LEXICAL SPECIFICATION 1.0

# A Proposed Lexicon for the Instrumental Observation of the Human Body

Six proposed English terms for describing the instruments, introduced agents, sensors, samplers, detectors, and readout systems through which the living human body becomes observable.

## 1. Purpose and scope

Modern medicine and human biology contain thousands of named devices and techniques, yet English lacks a concise vocabulary for the complete system by which the body is made physically knowable. Existing terms such as diagnostics, measurement, imaging, sensing, and sampling each cover only part of the territory.

The proposed lexicon distinguishes the total set of observational means, the field that studies that set, the body-specific practice of organizing the resulting knowledge, and the catalogs or repositories that preserve it.

## 2. Proposed lexical system

The six headwords are intentionally related without being interchangeable. Each occupies a distinct semantic role, allowing later usage to determine which terms prove most useful.

## 3. Headword specifications

## instrumentomics

/in-stru-men-TOM-iks/    noun, mass noun; grammatically singular

The systematic study and classification of instruments and other physical means used to make a subject or system observable.

Example: Human instrumentomics compares technologies according to what each makes observable.

Formation. Instrument plus the productive scientific suffix -omics, by analogy with fields concerned with a complete set of related entities.

Related forms. instrumentomic (adjective); instrumentome (noun)

Coinage status. Proposed as a new English headword. Preliminary exact-string research found no obvious established English use with this meaning at the date of publication.

## somagnomy

/so-MAG-nuh-mee/    noun

The systematic acquisition and organization of knowledge about the living body through physical observation and instrumentation.

Example: The exhibition traces the history of somagnomy from pulse taking to molecular imaging.

Formation. Greek soma, body, combined with -gnomy, relating to judgment or systematic knowing.

Related forms. somagnomic (adjective); somagnomist (noun)

Coinage status. Proposed as a new English headword. It is distinct from somatognosia, the neurological sense of bodily awareness or recognition.

## somatalogue

/so-MAT-uh-log/    noun

A systematic catalog or encyclopedia of instruments and methods used to observe the living body.

Example: The somatalogue organizes medical instruments by what they reveal rather than by clinical specialty.

Formation. A blend of soma, body, and catalogue.

Related forms. somatalogues (plural)

Coinage status. Proposed as a new English headword and as a possible generic description, not solely as a publication title or brand.

## somatheca

/so-muh-THEE-kuh/    noun

A physical or digital repository of instruments, methods, and records concerned with observing the living body.

Example: The digital somatheca preserves the history and operation of body-observing technologies.

Formation. Greek soma, body, combined with theke, a repository, container, or case.

Related forms. somathecae or somathecas (plural); somathecal (adjective)

Coinage status. Proposed as a new English headword. The term may describe a collection, archive, museum, or structured digital repository.

## somaphanics

/so-muh-FAN-iks/    noun, mass noun; grammatically singular

The science and practice of rendering bodily structures, conditions, or activities perceptible through instruments or introduced agents.

Example: Somaphanics includes electrical, acoustic, optical, chemical, and mechanical methods of observing the body.

Formation. Greek soma, body, combined with a root related to phainein, to show or make apparent, plus -ics.

Related forms. somaphanic (adjective)

Coinage status. Proposed as a new English headword. The related form somaphany has appeared in a separate poetic context and is not claimed here.

## instrumentome

/IN-stru-men-tohm/    noun

The complete set of instruments and other physical means through which a particular subject or system can be observed.

Example: The human instrumentome encompasses bedside tools, imaging systems, introduced tracers, implanted sensors, and laboratory samplers.

Formation. Instrument plus -ome, a suffix used for a complete set of related entities.

Related forms. instrumentomes (plural); instrumentomic (adjective); instrumentomics (noun)

Coinage status. Proposed as a specialized English sense rather than as the earliest appearance of the character string, which has isolated unrelated prior occurrences.

## 4. Usage, attribution, and revision

The terms are offered for general descriptive, scholarly, curatorial, and technical use. Their future meanings should be determined by genuine independent usage rather than by the authority of this document alone.

This specification records the proposal date and intended meanings. Individual words and short phrases are not ordinarily protected by copyright. Any use as a trademark or source identifier would require a separate legal analysis and should not be inferred from this document.

Later versions may clarify definitions, pronunciation, or relationships among terms. Versioned revisions should retain this first specification and its publication date so that the development of the vocabulary remains auditable.

## Suggested citation

Selberg, Kristoffer. A Proposed Lexicon for the Instrumental Observation of the Human Body. Version 1.0, 20 August 2026.

## Editorial note

This is a lexical proposal, not medical advice. Inclusion of a technology within the conceptual domain does not indicate safety, clinical effectiveness, regulatory authorization, or suitability for any person or purpose.
